facts.summary: Vermont's minimum wage is $14.42 per hour effective January 1, 2026, well above the federal $7.25, and is adjusted annually by the smaller of 5% or CPI-U.
facts.sourceAgency: Vermont Department of Labor, Wage & Hour Program
facts.notes: Figure taken from the official DOL 2026 Minimum Wage poster ($14.42 effective 01/01/2026; $14.01 in 2025; $13.67 in 2024). Rate re-indexes each January 1 under 21 V.S.A. § 384(a)(1).

facts.summary: Vermont's basic (tipped/service) wage for hotel, motel, tourist-place, and restaurant tipped employees is $7.21 per hour effective January 1, 2026 — one-half the full minimum wage.
facts.sourceAgency: Vermont Department of Labor, Wage & Hour Program
facts.notes: Statute sets the tipped basic wage at one-half the minimum wage; a 'service or tipped employee' is one who customarily receives more than $120/month in tips. Higher than the federal $2.13 tipped cash wage.

facts.value: follows federal FLSA (1.5x after 40 hrs/week; no general daily overtime)
facts.summary: Vermont requires 1.5x pay after 40 hours in a workweek like federal law, with no general daily-overtime rule; state OT law exempts several industries though FLSA may still cover them.
facts.notes: State OT threshold matches federal (40 hrs/week). Vermont's OT law expressly does NOT apply to retail/service establishments and to hotels, motels, and restaurants (21 V.S.A. § 384(b)(1)-(3)); a daily-OT election exists only for certain healthcare facilities (§ 384(b)(4)). Federal FLSA overtime may still cover employees exempted from the state provision.

facts.summary: Vermont's Fair Employment Practices Act protects several classes beyond the federal set, including sexual orientation, gender identity, ancestry, place of birth, crime victim status, and HIV-related test status.
facts.notes: Full statutory list also includes race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age, and disability (mirroring federal). Vermont's age protection is not limited to workers 40+ as under the federal ADEA. HIV-related blood-test discrimination is separately barred at § 495(a)(5)-(6).

facts.summary: Vermont's anti-discrimination law covers any employer with one or more individuals performing services in the state, far below the federal 15-employee (Title VII/ADA) threshold.
facts.notes: The statutory 'employer' definition reaches any entity 'that has one or more individuals performing services for it within this State.'

facts.value: no administrative-charge deadline; private suit directly in Superior Court within the 6-year civil limitations period
facts.summary: Unlike the EEOC's 180/300-day charge deadline, Vermont lets an aggrieved employee sue directly in Superior Court without first filing an administrative charge, subject to the state's general 6-year statute of limitations.
facts.notes: § 495b(b) grants a private right of action in Superior Court with no exhaustion requirement. The 6-year period comes from Vermont's general civil statute of limitations (12 V.S.A. § 511); confirm the applicable limitations period for a specific claim, as courts may apply a different period to some theories. The Attorney General or a State's Attorney may also enforce (§ 495b(a)).

facts.summary: Wage claims in Vermont are governed by the state's general six-year civil statute of limitations.
facts.notes: Vermont's wage-and-hour subchapter has no dedicated limitations period, so the general 6-year civil SOL applies. Verify against current case law for the specific wage theory (e.g., minimum wage vs. contract-based claims).

facts.value: prohibited for wage/hour complaints and cooperation
facts.summary: Vermont bars employers from discharging or retaliating against employees for lodging, or being expected to lodge, a wage-and-hour complaint or for cooperating in a Commissioner investigation.
facts.notes: Aggrieved employees may sue in Superior Court for compensatory and punitive damages, reinstatement, restitution, costs, and attorney's fees. Separate anti-retaliation protection for discrimination complaints exists at 21 V.S.A. § 495(a)(8).

facts.value: written anti-harassment policy required of all employers
facts.summary: Vermont requires every employer to adopt a written sexual-harassment policy meeting statutory content requirements — an obligation with no direct federal counterpart.
facts.notes: Policy must state that harassment is unlawful, describe examples and consequences, and (for employers with more than five employees) describe the complaint process. Statute also limits mandatory-arbitration and NDA provisions related to harassment.

facts.value: protected for health care employees (hospitals and nursing homes)
facts.summary: Vermont provides statutory whistleblower protection to hospital and nursing-home employees who report improper quality of patient care or violations of law.
facts.notes: This subchapter covers health care employees only (hospitals per 18 V.S.A. § 1902(1); nursing homes per 33 V.S.A. § 7102(7)). Vermont's general whistleblower statute for State employees is at 3 V.S.A. §§ 971-978 (not captured here). No single general private-sector whistleblower statute was located.

facts.value: discharge: within 72 hours; resignation: next regular payday (or following Friday if none)
facts.summary: Vermont requires a discharged employee to be paid within 72 hours of discharge; an employee who voluntarily leaves is paid on the last regular payday, or the following Friday if there is no regular payday.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary statute text. Also covers the (rarer) case of an employee absent on the regular payday, who is entitled to payment upon demand under 342(b)(3).
